source_text: Numquid non idem, Adimantus et Faustus (quem in libris Confessionis tuae praeceptorem tuum loqueris [n21] ), haeresiarchae sui traditione fecerunt, obscuriores quasque vel de Evangelio, vel de Apostolorum Epistolis sententias rapientes et corro ntes, ut profanum dogma nominum auctoritate tuerentur? Quamquam quid dico de Manichaeis? Omnes prorsus haereses inventa sua, quibus a pietate et fide exorbitaverunt, Scripturarum elocutionibus sententiisque communiunt.
pass_a_gloss: Did not the same Adimantus and Faustus (whom in the books of your Confession you speak of as your teacher), by the tradition of their heresiarch, do this, seizing and gnawing the more obscure sentences, whether from the Gospel or from the Apostles' Letters, that they might guard a profane dogma by the authority of names? And yet why do I speak of the Manichaeans? All heresies outright fortify their inventions, by which they have veered from piety and faith, with the expressions and sentences of the Scriptures.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil

pass_b_english: Did not Adimantus and Faustus, whom you call your teacher in the books of your Confessions, do the same thing, following the tradition of their heresy's founder (Augustine, Confessions 5.6–7, 13)? They seized and gnawed away at whatever statements were more obscure, whether from the Gospel or the apostles' letters, to defend an impious doctrine through the authority of those names. But why speak only of the Manichaeans? Every heresy fortifies its own inventions, through which it has strayed from piety and faith, with the language and statements of Scripture.

choices.why: Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

variants.reading: The source's broken “corro ntes” is read as corrodentes, “gnawing away”, in parallel with “seizing”.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
